title: More parameters than data
objectives: Explain the second fall in test error once parameters outnumber data points.

screens.title: More features than points
screens.prose: We fit 40 noisy points (10 inputs, a linear signal plus noise) by least squares on $p$ random ReLU features, for $p$ from 5 to 200. When $p > 40$ there are many exact fits, and we take the one with the smallest weights.
screens.question: Predict the test error as $p$ grows, then reveal the chart.

options.text: It rises to a peak near $p = 40$, then falls again
It keeps rising: more parameters, more overfitting
options.why: Past the peak it falls: 0.388 at $p = 200$ against 11.0 at 40.

options.text: It keeps falling: bigger models always do better
A single U with its bottom near $p = 40$
options.why: The bottom of the first U is well below 40; 40 is the worst point.

hints.text: At $p = 40$ there are as many features as points.
One exact fit, forced through every noisy point.
Past 40 the smallest-weight fit is gentler.

feedback.correct: Double descent: 0.874 at $p = 10$, 11.0 at 40, 0.388 at 200 on this seed.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Reveal both curves and read the peak.

byKey.up: That is the half-truth: the peak is real, but the error falls again past it.
byKey.down: That is the mirror half-truth: the peak shows bigger is not always better.

explain.text: The error peaks at $p = n$, then falls as $p$ grows: **double descent**. With a small ridge penalty (dashed) the peak is gone: 0.913 at 40.

screens.title: Which exact fit?
screens.prose: Name it: past the **interpolation threshold** $p = n$, the equations $\mathbf{F}\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{y}$ have infinitely many solutions. The **minimum-norm** one, $\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{F}^+\mathbf{y}$ (`eigen` l17's pseudoinverse), picks the one with the smallest $\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert$. A one-row example: $w_1 + w_2 = 2$.
screens.question: What is $w_1$ in the minimum-norm solution?

hints.text: Every solution has $w_2 = 2 - w_1$.
The minimum is at $w_1 = 1$.

feedback.correct: $w = (1, 1)$, with norm $\sqrt 2$; any other solution, such as $(2, 0)$, is longer.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Minimise the length along the line $w_1 + w_2 = 2$.

byKey.one: $(2, 0)$ is a solution, but its norm is 2; $(1, 1)$ has norm $\sqrt 2$.

explain.text: The shortest point on the line $w_1 + w_2 = 2$ is its foot from the origin, $(1, 1)$, which is $\mathbf{F}^+\mathbf{y}$ for $\mathbf{F} = (1, 1)$.

screens.title: A small penalty removes the peak
screens.prose: The dashed curve adds a ridge penalty $\lambda = 0.1$. At $p = n$ the matrix $\mathbf{F}$ is square and badly conditioned (`numerics` l3, if you have it), so the exact fit swings wildly; the penalty refuses those large weights.
screens.question: What is the ridge test error at $p = 40$ on this seed? Give 3 decimal places.

hints.text: Read the dashed curve at the vertical line.
It sits near 0.91.
Compare with the solid curve's spike.

feedback.correct: 0.913, against 11.0 for the exact minimum-norm fit.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the dashed curve at $p = 40$.

byKey.mn: That is the solid curve, with no penalty.
byKey.end: That is the ridge curve at $p = 200$.

explain.text: The penalty caps the weights where $\mathbf{F}$ is nearly singular, so the error at $p = 40$ drops from 11.0 to 0.913. The peak moves and shrinks with the noise and the penalty.

screens.title: Square and badly conditioned
screens.prose: The condition number of $\mathbf{F}$, its largest singular value over its smallest, measures how much the fit can amplify noise in $\mathbf{y}$. The table gives it for five feature counts.

state.caption: Largest over smallest singular value of the 40-row feature matrix, seed 0.

screens.question: At which $p$ is $\mathbf{F}$ worst conditioned?

hints.text: Find the largest number in the table.
That is where $\mathbf{F}$ is square.

feedback.correct: At $p = 40$: 4,095, against 71 at 30 and 115 at 50. A square random matrix almost always has some tiny singular value.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the largest condition number.

byKey.few: With 10 features the fit has room to spare and the matrix is well conditioned.
byKey.many: With 200 features there are many directions to share the fit.

explain.text: At $p = n = 40$ the smallest singular value is tiny, so the condition number is 4,095 and the exact fit amplifies the noise: the spike in the error. Past it, the extra features add room and the number falls.

screens.title: Bigger is always better?
screens.prose: Una reads the chart and concludes the opposite of the textbook: since the error falls past $p = 40$, bigger models are always better and regularisation is unnecessary.
screens.question: What is wrong?

options.text: The peak is real and moves; a penalty stays the safer default
Nothing: past the threshold more features always help
options.why: At $p = 40$ more features made it far worse, and other seeds peak at slightly different $p$.

options.text: The fall past 40 is a fluke of one seed
options.why: All five seeds peak near 40 and fall again; the fall is not luck.

options.text: The textbook is right: more parameters always overfit more
options.why: The fall past the peak contradicts that.

hints.text: Is the curve monotone anywhere?
It rises, peaks, then falls.
Neither "always worse" nor "always better" fits.

feedback.correct: Both slogans fail: the error peaks at the threshold, and a small penalty removes the peak at little cost.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Describe the whole curve.

byKey.right: That is the mirror misconception: the peak shows that more is not always better.
byKey.textbook: That is the classical half: it misses the second fall.

explain.text: Double descent licenses neither slogan. Near $p = n$ the minimum-norm fit is dangerous; a small ridge penalty gives low error at every $p$.

screens.title: Small weights by default
screens.prose: Among all exact fits, the minimum-norm one is the gentlest. Gradient descent on least squares from zero weights converges to exactly that fit, $\mathbf{w}_\infty = \mathbf{F}^+\mathbf{y}$; for big nets trained from small weights, a similar pull towards small-norm fits is an observed tendency, not a theorem.
screens.question: Gradient descent from $\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}$ on an underdetermined least-squares problem converges to which solution?

options.text: The minimum-norm solution $\mathbf{F}^+\mathbf{y}$
Some exact solution, depending on the step size
options.why: From zero, every step lies in the row space of $\mathbf{F}$, so the limit is the minimum-norm one.

options.text: None: it diverges when there are many solutions
options.why: With a small enough step it converges.

options.text: A ridge solution
options.why: It fits exactly; ridge does not.

hints.text: Each gradient is a combination of the rows of $\mathbf{F}$.
So the weights stay in the row space.
The only exact fit there is $\mathbf{F}^+\mathbf{y}$.

feedback.correct: The minimum-norm solution: steps from zero never leave the row space of $\mathbf{F}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Where do the gradient steps point?

explain.text: Every gradient $\mathbf{F}^T(\mathbf{F}\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{y})$ is in the row space, and the one exact fit inside it is $\mathbf{F}^+\mathbf{y}$.

screens.title: Double descent in code
screens.prose: Write `random_relu_features(X, p, seed)`, `min_norm_fit(F, y)` and `double_descent_curve(ps, n, noise, seed)` as the starter's comments say. The number script checks five seeds; the hidden tests check the shape on two of them.
screens.question: Complete the three functions.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np


def random_relu_features(X, p, seed):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    W = np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal((X.shape[1], p)) / np.sqrt(X.shape[1])
    return np.maximum(X @ W, 0)


def min_norm_fit(F, y):
    return np.linalg.pinv(np.asarray(F, dtype=float)) @ np.asarray(y, dtype=float)


def double_descent_curve(ps, n, noise, seed):
    g = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    beta = g.standard_normal(10)
    beta /= np.linalg.norm(beta)
    Xa = g.standard_normal((n, 10))
    ya = Xa @ beta + noise * g.standard_normal(n)
    Xs = g.standard_normal((2000, 10))
    ys = Xs @ beta
    out = []
    for p in ps:
        F = random_relu_features(np.vstack([Xa, Xs]), p, seed + 1000)
        w = min_norm_fit(F[:n], ya)
        out.append(float(np.mean((F[n:] @ w - ys) ** 2)))
    return out

import numpy as np


def random_relu_features(X, p, seed):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    W = np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal((X.shape[1], p)) / np.sqrt(X.shape[1])
    return np.maximum(X @ W, 0)

        w = min_norm_fit(F[:n], ya)

screens.title: More factors than months
screens.prose: A quant has 120 candidate factors and 60 months of returns. A minimum-norm least-squares fit can match every month exactly and still predict sensibly; double descent says it is not automatically a disaster.
screens.question: What is the safer default, and why?

options.text: A ridge penalty chosen on validation months
The minimum-norm fit: past the threshold it is always fine
options.why: Fine on average past the peak, but near $p = n$ it swings wildly, and the peak moves with the noise.

options.text: Cut to 59 factors, just below the threshold
options.why: Just below the threshold is where the error is worst.

options.text: Use all 120 with plain least squares
options.why: Plain least squares has no unique answer here; some rule must pick one.

hints.text: Where is the danger in the curve?
Near $p = n$.
Ridge flattened the peak.

feedback.correct: A ridge penalty, chosen on validation months, is low at every number of factors.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which fit was safe across the whole curve?

explain.text: The minimum-norm fit can be good past the peak but is dangerous near it, and the peak moves. Ridge removed it at every $p$ in our runs.

ideas: Test error against the number of random features rises to a peak at $p = n$ and falls again: double descent (11.0 at 40, 0.388 at 200 on seed 0).
Past the threshold there are infinitely many exact fits; the pseudoinverse picks the minimum-norm one, which gradient descent from zero also finds.
A small ridge penalty removes the peak (0.913 at 40); neither "bigger always overfits" nor "bigger is always better" holds.
